method: Aerobic decoupling compares how much speed a steady session produced per heartbeat in its first and second halves. The efficiency factor is speed divided by average heart rate: speed is the half's distance in metres divided by its duration in minutes, so the factor is in metres per minute per beat, and heart rate is the half's average in bpm. Decoupling is (first-half factor - second-half factor) / first-half factor x 100, so a positive value means the second half produced less speed per beat than the first, and a negative value means heart rate fell relative to the output. Pace is the half's duration per unit of distance, rounded to the nearest second. The 5% and 10% band edges are inclusive on the lower side: 5.0% or less is reported as coupled, just over 5% up to 10% as moderate drift, and above 10% as high drift, with the same sizes labelled negative drift when the sign is negative. Distances are converted with 1 km = 1,000 m and 1 mi = 1,609.344 m. Durations are accepted as MM:SS or H:MM:SS between 1:00 and 10:00:00, distances between 0.1 and 1,000 in the chosen unit, and average heart rates between 40 and 250 bpm. The figure is only meaningful when the halves are comparable: same route or trainer, similar terrain and cadence, steady effort, no stops, and consistent fuelling. Heat, dehydration, caffeine, illness and poor sleep raise heart rate without any loss of fitness, and a harder first half lowers the second-half efficiency factor for the same reason, so a single session is a signal and a repeated pattern is the trend. This is a training-analysis figure, not a medical measurement or a prediction of performance. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Allen, H. and Coggan, A., Training and Racing with a Power Meter: introduces the efficiency factor (speed or power divided by heart rate) and the Pw:HR decoupling comparison between the halves of a steady ride.

Coggan, A., aerobic decoupling (Pa:HR) guidance in the TrainingPeaks/WKO documentation: the 5% threshold for the second half of a steady aerobic session once warm-up is excluded, with larger values read as aerobic decoupling.
Friel, J., The Triathlete's Training Bible: decoupling of pace from heart rate as an aerobic-base and durability marker in endurance training.

Coyle, E. F. and Gonzalez-Alonso, J. (2001), Cardiovascular drift during prolonged exercise: new perspectives, Exercise and Sport Sciences Reviews 29(2):88-92: heart rate rises and stroke volume falls during prolonged steady exercise, so pace per beat declines without a change in fitness.

Sawka, M. N. et al. (2007), ACSM position stand: Exercise and fluid replacement, Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise 39(2):377-390: dehydration and heat increase cardiovascular strain and heart rate at a fixed workload.
